messages.author: 87d6a01c1ab6ddf0
messages.subject: Priors for Stochastic Volatility
parts:
In the stochastic volatility model in Section 6.5 of the manual (version 2.8.0), the prior for the volatility of the log volatility {{sigma}} is given as a Cauchy distribution. But this parameter should be strictly positive and in fact there is a constraint to ensure that it is positive. What happens to invalid samples? Is there rejection sampling going on under the covers? Wouldn't it better to choose e.g a Gamma distribution with shape = 0.5 and rate = 0.005 to avoid this?

Dominic.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Priors for Stochastic Volatility
parts:
On Sunday, November 8, 2015 at 12:34:00 PM UTC-5, Dominic Steinitz wrote:
In the stochastic volatility model in Section 6.5 of the manual (version 2.8.0), the prior for the volatility of the log volatility {{sigma}} is given as a Cauchy distribution. But this parameter should be strictly positive and in fact there is a constraint to ensure that it is positive. What happens to invalid samples? Is there rejection sampling going on under the covers?

There are almost surely no invalid samples to reject due to Stan's hidden transformations. The declaration in the parameters block that

real<lower=0> sigma;

implies that sigma is actually exp(log_sigma) but you don't declare / define / see log_sigma and Stan handle Jacobian term for you for anything declared in the parameters block (only).

The prior

sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);

places a CONSTANT amount of density on the negative part of the real line where sigma cannot be. So, conceptually this should be a truncated prior

sigma ~ cauchy(0,5) T[0,];

However, the truncation would only subtract the CONSTANT log(1 - 0.5) from the log-posterior, and constants do not affect which proposals get accepted or rejected by the Metropolis test. So, including the truncation would only slow things down and not affect any of the posterior draws. In effect, this amounts to a half-Cauchy prior over the positive numbers.

But, it is far too easy to utilize this shortcut when it is not appropriate; namely, in situations where the median and / or scale of the Cauchy distribution are unknowns in which case the amount of truncated density is not a constant. In those situations, you should either truncate explicitly or use a distribution that is defined for a non-negative variable.
Wouldn't it better to choose e.g a Gamma distribution with shape = 0.5 and rate = 0.005 to avoid this?

We have mostly stopped advocating Cauchy priors but don't like Gamma priors with such a small rate (or shape) either. It isn't technically necessary to use a prior that is defined only for positive numbers but whether you get efficient sampling for a particular choice of prior also depends a lot on the data.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Priors for Stochastic Volatility
parts:
Excellent reply - thanks very much.

The only reason I used a Gamma with those parameters is because this suggests it (Section 2.2). Left to my own devices I would probably have chosen something like

  sigma ~ lognormal(0.25,1.0);

Is this shortcut documented somewhere? It might be worth adding a note to the manual if not.

> Excellent reply - thanks very much.

> The only reason I used a Gamma with those parameters is because this suggests it (Section 2.2).

Most direct implementations of Gibbs samplers choose
conjugate priors for convenience, such as the inverse
gamma on variance they suggest in that vignette.

> Left to my own devices I would probably have chosen something like
>
> sigma ~ lognormal(0.25,1.0);
>
> Is this shortcut documented somewhere? It might be worth adding a note to the manual if not.

I'm not sure what you mean by "shortcut" here. The manual explains
that you don't need the truncation if the contribution would be constant.
But there are multiple issues like this (especially the necessity of
constraints in the first place) that are hard to make sure people read
before they start trying to code.

- Bob
